papers.title: Multi-hazard climate hazard exposure and livestock vulnerability in Nepal: a district-level spatial risk assessment
papers.summary: Abstract Livestock-dependent livelihoods across Nepal face escalating multi-hazard climate exposure yet remain absent from national risk assessments and early warning frameworks. This study presents the district-level spatial assessment integrating biophysical hazard exposure with livestock-specific social vulnerability across all 77 administrative districts using a 2000–2023 baseline. We construct a five-hazard Multi-Hazard Exposure Index (MHEI: flood, drought, landslide, low temperature exposure frequency, high temperature exposure frequency) and a four-dimension Livestock Vulnerability Index (LVI: livestock dependence, poverty, veterinary access, social marginalization), classify districts through bivariate spatial overlay, and assess geographic clustering using Global Moran’s I . Compound risk is concentrated in 37 districts (48%), forming a statistically significant spatial cluster (Moran’s I = 0.41, E [ I ] = −0.013, z = 4.87, p < 0.001) across Sudurpashchim and mid-western hills, with Achham, Doti, Bajura, Bajhang, and Pyuthan as highest-priority districts. Absolute hazard intensity and compound risk are spatially uncoupled: highest MHEI values occur in central-western mountain districts, while highest compound risk emerges where moderate hazard intersects deep structural vulnerability in the far west. Composite risk scores show significant directional agreement with recorded livestock losses from Nepal’s BIPAD portal (Spearman’s ρ = 0.239, p = 0.037), providing empirical corroboration of the framework.

papers.title: MULTIMODAL DISCOURSE ANALYSIS BASED ON INDONESIAN NATIONAL CHARACTER VALUES IN ENGLISH-LANGUAGE DISASTER-RELATED TEXTS: RELATIONSHIPS AMONG WORDS, IMAGES, AND LAYOUT
papers.source: Journal of Education Technology and Civic Literacy (JET CIVIL)
papers.summary: This article aims to develop a multimodal discourse analysis framework grounded in Indonesian national character values to examine relationships among verbal, visual, and layout elements in English-language disaster texts, focusing on the flash floods and landslides in North Sumatra in late 2025. This conceptual-analytical study employs a narrative literature review of multimodality theory, systemic functional linguistics, critical discourse analysis, character education values stipulated in Presidential Regulation Number 87 of 2017, and relevant previous studies. The findings propose a framework integrating word–image relationships, layout organization, and their implications for message clarity and disaster risk communication. The framework also identifies representations of religiosity, social awareness, environmental concern, responsibility, discipline, national spirit, and patriotism through linguistic choices, visual representations, and page composition. Additionally, a five-step analytical protocol and corpus selection criteria are formulated to support future empirical investigations. The study's novelty lies in integrating multimodal discourse analysis with national character indicators within English-language disaster communication. However, as no empirical corpus analysis has been conducted, the proposed framework and analytical protocol remain conceptual and require further empirical validation.

papers.title: Can extreme rainfall associated with landslides affect air quality? A case study in a coastal city (São Sebastião, São Paulo State, Brazil)
papers.summary: Abstract This study investigated the impact of an extreme precipitation event and the subsequent landslides that occurred in São Sebastião municipality (São Paulo State, Brazil) in February 2023 on particulate matter (PM 10 and PM 2.5 ) concentration. Hourly air quality and meteorological data from December 2021 to February 2025 were analyzed. The methodology combined cluster analysis (CA) using the k -means algorithm to classify meteorological patterns and the Openair package for spatio-temporal assessment. CA identified a specific group of days associated with anomalous behavior during the extreme event. Analyses using bivariate polar plots and variation in time plots revealed that, while intense rainfall initially promoted wet scavenging of pollutants, the post-landslide period was characterized by a 124% increase in PM 10 concentrations and a 93.3% increase in PM 2.5 concentrations. Two additional high precipitation events were examined for comparison, showing that PM also decreased during intense rainfall, while the post-rainfall recovery differed among events. These results indicate that the February 2023 increase cannot be explained by landslide occurrence alone and may have reflected the combined influence of meteorological conditions, changes in local activities, and potential particle resuspension . Overall, the findings highlight the importance of adequate monitoring networks in place for understanding the secondary environmental effects of extreme rainfall and disaster events in vulnerable coastal areas.

papers.title: Long-Term Seepage and Stability of Tropical Railway Cut Slopes Using Satellite Hydroclimatic Data
papers.summary: Abstract Rainfall-induced landslides threaten tropical railway infrastructure, where sparse monitoring limits the characterization of rainfall–instability relationships. This study investigated the long-term hydraulic response and stability of railway cut slopes in residual soils along a strategic railway in the Brazilian Amazon using alternative climate datasets. Satellite-derived precipitation (CHIRPS), satellite-informed soil moisture (SMAP), and gridded meteorological variables (BR-DWGD) were integrated with laboratory hydraulic relationships and field groundwater observations to define atmospheric forcing and initial hydraulic conditions. Daily sequential seepage–stability simulations spanning more than 40 yrs were performed for four representative slope inclinations. Increasing inclination reduced stability, and only the 40° slope exhibited simulated instability. Mean annual precipitation was highest during La Niña, intermediate during neutral conditions, and lowest during El Niño, whereas mean annual minimum factor of safety (FoS) followed the reverse ordering across all inclinations. Statistically significant differences supported an association between El Niño–Southern Oscillation variability and simulated stability. Mean monthly minimum FoS was lowest in April for steeper slopes, consistent with cumulative wet-season infiltration and broadly aligned with reported March–April slope-instability events along the railway. A criterion combining 7-, 15-, and 90-day rainfall accumulations provided a preliminary model-derived reference for investigating simulated instability. The underlying mechanisms involved matric suction dissipation and localized groundwater rise near the toe, without requiring full saturation of the overlying soil. Hydraulic contrasts can guide instrumentation placement. Peer Review Report For: From Separation to Synergy: A Systematic Literature Review on Machine Learning–IoT Integration for Disaster Risk Management [version 1; peer review: 1 approved]
papers.summary: Natural disasters such as earthquakes, floods, landslides, and wildfires continue to increase in frequency and impact globally, necessitating risk management systems that are faster, more accurate, and based on real-time data. Machine Learning (ML) and the Internet of Things (IoT) are widely used to support disaster prediction, early detection, and mitigation; however, most research still treats these two technologies separately, so patterns of ML–IoT collaboration have not yet been systematically studied. This study employs a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) approach following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines to map trends, approaches, and challenges in the integration of ML and IoT for disaster risk management. The search was conducted in the ScienceDirect, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and Springer databases, yielding 533 initial records that were filtered down to 402 relevant articles; ultimately, 91 articles met all inclusion criteria for in-depth analysis. The study’s results indicate that deep learning is the most widely used approach (36.3%), with floods (36.3%) and landslides (23.1%) being the most frequently studied types of disasters. IoT sensors were identified as the dominant data source (42.9%), while early warning systems were the most commonly implemented ML–IoT integration architecture (34.1%). Nevertheless, the integration of ML and IoT within a single, cohesive framework remains relatively limited, and the main challenges identified include model accuracy and generalization, limitations in data quality, and the lack of maturity in operational aspects such as scalability, interoperability, and IoT device energy consumption. These findings underscore the need for further research focused on a more holistic ML–IoT integration that is ready for operational implementation in disaster risk management.

Hydrodynamic loads on tandem twin pipelines induced by submarine landslides: Insights from physical flume tests and SPH simulations
papers.summary: Submarine landslides impose extreme dynamic hazards on subsea pipelines. Research concerning the fluid-structure interaction between submarine landslides and tandem twin pipelines remains limited. In this work, flume model tests are performed using slurries consisting of sand, kaolin clay and water to reproduce landslide masses. A validated multiphase smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) model is adopted to quantify the influences of landslide volume, slope gradient, solid mass fraction and pipeline geometry on impact loads and wake-shielding performance. The full landslide-impact process is categorized into four successive stages: initial collision, main peak loading, steady impact, and deposition dissipation. When subjected to submarine-landslide impact, the upstream pipeline generates a flow-blocking shielding effect for its downstream counterpart, delaying the downstream impact response and substantially lowering its peak impact load. At a solid mass fraction of 70%, the load reduction ratio attains 62.18% for an upstream-pipeline diameter of 30 mm and further rises to 85.47% at 50 mm. A critical “most unfavorable spacing” is identified; this characteristic spacing shift downstream from 250 mm to 350 mm as the landslide volume increases from 0.024 m 3 to 0.040 m 3 . The present findings provide theoretical references for disaster-resistant layout design of subsea pipelines.

papers.title: Human Security-Based Ipas Learning For Strengthening Disaster Mitigation Awareness: A Literature Review
papers.summary: Indonesia is highly vulnerable to natural disasters, particularly hydrometeorological events such as floods and landslides. Preliminary interviews at SD Negeri Kebalen 05 indicated that most fifth-grade students had limited understanding of disaster preparedness beyond earthquakes, despite the school’s flood-prone geographical location. This condition highlights the need to integrate disaster mitigation education into IPAS (Natural and Social Sciences) learning through a human security approach emphasizing safety, well-being, and sustainability. This study aims to examine how human security-based IPAS learning contributes to students’ understanding of disaster mitigation concepts and warning signs. A qualitative approach using a narrative literature review was employed. Relevant scientific articles, books, and research reports published between 2016 and 2026 were retrieved from Google Scholar, SINTA, and DOAJ. An initial search identified 42 records using keywords related to human security, disaster mitigation, and IPAS learning. Following title and abstract screening, full-text eligibility assessment, and methodological review, 21 studies were included in the final synthesis. Data were analyzed using descriptive qualitative content analysis. The findings indicate that human security-based IPAS learning can strengthen students’ knowledge, attitudes, and disaster preparedness skills, providing a foundation for developing adaptive and inclusive IPAS learning while supporting SDG 4 (Quality Education) in elementary schools.

papers.title: Fuzzy logic and frequency ratio based landslide susceptibility mapping using geo environmental and hydro meteorological factors in pithoragarh, uttarakhand
papers.summary: Mass movement events leads to severe infrastructural and socioeconomic damage across the Himalayan belt, particularly in Pithoragarh, Uttarakhand, India, where over nearly 1,000 events have been recorded in the last two decades. Modelling landslide susceptibility in such highly several, monsoon dominated terrains requires frameworks capable of handling significant spatial and lithological uncertainty. This study assesses and map out regional landslide vulnerability using a Multi Criteria Decision Analysis methodology based on fuzzy logic and frequency ratio. A spatial database comprising fourteen geo spatial and hydro meteorological conditioning factors was integrated to capture the region’s complex topographical and climatic changes. The analytical performances of the models were mathematically validated against a historical landslide inventory using the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve. For this uncertain terrain, the Fuzzy Logic model produced a realistic and reliable susceptibility standard with an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.686, in the other hand the frequency ratio model provides an AUC of 0.876. In this region, the middle and southern part, which are dominated by unconsolidated soils and heavy monsoon precipitation, are major hazard zones, while the northern side crystalline rock formations are still mostly stable, according to the spatial distribution analysis. So, this verified that the Frequency ratio hazard zonation map offers a data driven, optimal decision support tool compared to fuzzy logic for infrastructure development and disaster risk assessment.

papers.title: A rapid remote sensing monitoring method for geologic hazards based on multi-UAV collaboration
papers.summary: Monitoring geologic hazards in an emergency situation presents challenges related to inadequate coverage and insufficient response speed. Balancing efficiency and accuracy is difficult with traditional remote sensing technology. This problem is addressed by proposing a multi-unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-based remote monitoring method for geologic hazards. To achieve this, a layered system architecture is designed to integrate distributed task allocation and an artificial potential field mechanism for avoiding obstacles. Additionally, a multi-source data fusion process is constructed and a deep-learning network for semantic segmentation is adopted to intelligently identify landslide hazards. Finally, differential interferometry is used to monitor ground subsidence. Results from experimental validation demonstrate that the method offers significant enhancements in terms of monitoring efficiency, recognition accuracy, and cost control. It also provides technical backup for geological disaster emergency response.

papers.title: Slope-unit-based GIS-AHP modelling for geological hazard susceptibility and construction suitability mapping
papers.summary: This study presents an integrated remote sensing and GIS-based workflow for geohazard mapping and construction suitability zoning in the Yunyang Economic Development Zone, Hubei Province, China. High-resolution satellite image interpretation, DEM-derived terrain analysis, field investigation, soil geochemical sampling, electrical resistivity tomography, and exploratory drilling were integrated within a unified GIS database to extract geo-geological information and support spatial assessment. Using 1:10,000 mapping and slope-unit delineation, 603 slope units were generated and 29 geological hazard sites were identified, including 24 landslides and 5 rockfalls, threatening 486 households and 1,744 residents. An AHP-based susceptibility model classified 10.72% of the study area as very high susceptibility and 21.16% as high susceptibility, mainly in steep terrain with unfavorable geological conditions. Subsequent hazard-vulnerability integration produced a risk map with 9.12% extremely high-risk, 23.39% high-risk, 44.80% medium-risk, and 22.68% low-risk zones. GIS-based construction suitability mapping further divided the study area into suitable (12.52%), restricted (28.97%), and prohibited (58.51%) zones. The results show that integrating remote sensing interpretation, digital mapping, and GIS-based multi-factor analysis provides an effective approach for geo-geological information extraction, geohazard zoning, and spatial planning in mountainous development areas.

papers.title: An integrated method for deformation monitoring of reservoir landslides using multisource data and its application
papers.summary: To address the critical challenge of bank landslide disaster prevention and control within reservoir operations, this paper proposes an integrated “space-air” landslide deformation monitoring methodology. This approach synergistically combines Synthetic Aperture Radar Interferometry (InSAR) and UAV tilt photogrammetry. SAR satellite data are utilized for the identification of widespread, latent hazards and for conducting time-series deformation monitoring of disaster-prone sites within the reservoir area. Concurrently, UAV tilt photogrammetry is employed to generate high-precision 3D real-scene models of landslides, enabling the calculation of their three-dimensional deformation. The fusion and analysis of these multi-source monitoring data are achieved through heterogeneous data registration. Application to the Kaiting Landslide, located in a hydropower station reservoir area in Southwest China, demonstrates the integrated InSAR and UAV technology’s efficacy in significantly enhancing landslide monitoring reliability. This methodology offers robust technical support for the safety management and early warning systems of reservoir bank landslides.

papers.title: Combined spaceborne and ground-based InSAR for deformation monitoring of portal slopes of long-span highway tunnel
papers.summary: Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) technology has been widely adopted for deformation monitoring of transportation infrastructure. However, monitoring alpine high-altitude mountain tunnels remains challenging due to complex geology and frequent landslides. Conventional single InSAR techniques suffer from monitoring blind zones caused by terrain layover and shadow, and only provide one-dimensional deformation data, failing to simultaneously implement large-scale hazard screening and high-precision real-time tunnel portal monitoring. This paper proposes a multi-level deformation monitoring framework integrating space-borne InSAR, ground-based InSAR and LiDAR. First, ascending and descending orbit SBAS-InSAR integrated with SAR geometric visibility analysis is adopted to remove layover and shadow distortion areas. A dual-orbit 2D deformation inversion model is constructed to retrieve vertical and east-west deformation fields along the tunnel alignment, enabling macroscopic full-scale screening of hidden geological hazards. Subsequently, ground-based InSAR is fused with 3D LiDAR, and a multi-criteria hierarchical PS point screening framework is established to improve the precision of monitoring targets via multi-constraint optimization. Coordinate registration and 3D projection algorithms are applied to realize accurate 3D visualization of one-dimensional slope deformation data. Finally, experimental validation is conducted based on an extra-long alpine high-altitude tunnel in Xinjiang. The proposed method accurately identifies high-risk tunnel portal areas and captures real-time millimeter-scale local micro-deformations at tunnel portals. Validations demonstrate that the integrated monitoring method adapts to harsh mountainous monitoring environments and integrates advantages of large-area general survey and high-precision local detailed measurement, providing solid technical support for slope disaster prevention during construction and operation of mount

papers.title: From the mountains to the sky: Aerial Cable-Cars lifting social inclusion and transport equity in Latin America
papers.summary: Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC) is a region with deep transport and spatial inequalities, producing differences in travel behaviour and transport supply across communities, as people living in the peripheries experience longer travel times and costs to access essential amenities. Topography is another important factor exacerbating these inequalities, as many LAC settlements are located near the Andes Mountains. Disadvantaged communities (DC) in the region are usually located in hilly terrain, often in areas at risk of landslides, and are characterised by informal development. In this context, Aerial Cable-Cars (ACC) presents a mode of public transport that provides high-quality service and infrastructure in LAC cities with the potential to improve social inclusion and accessibility for vulnerable communities. ACC have been rapidly adopted throughout LAC since their first introduction in Medellín in 2004. And particularly after 2010, when more than 90% of operational ACCs were inaugurated. This thesis seeks to contribute to the understanding of ACC technology as a mode of transport in LAC urban settlements, along with its implications for activity participation and transport-related social exclusion (TRSE), accessibility and transport equity, and mode choice. To do so, the study first conducted a literature review of empirical evidence on ACC transport projects in LAC. Then, the thesis focused on two case studies in Colombia: Bogotá and Manizales. In Bogotá, the first ACC (TransMiCable) was inaugurated in 2018, connecting Ciudad Bolívar’s residents to the Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) system and primarily serving as a feeder. In Manizales, the ACC system (Cable Aéreo) comprises three interconnected lines, inaugurated in 2009, 2014, and 2025.

papers.title: Research on identification and assessment techniques for collapse-landslide disasters in Southeastern Tibet
papers.summary: The southeastern Tibet region lies at the collision front between the Indian Plate and the Eurasian Plate, characterized by intense tectonic activity, dense fault networks, fragmented rock masses, and complex conditions conducive to disasters such as landslides and collapses due to heavy precipitation, earthquakes, freeze-thaw cycles, and engineering disturbances. This study establishes a comprehensive technical framework integrating optical remote sensing interpretation, radar-based deformation detection, field verification, and susceptibility assessment, guided by the principle of "identification– evaluation–application." The research covers an area of approximately 180,000 km², identifying over 54,000 historical geological hazard sites through optical interpretation and detecting more than 60,000 potential hazards via radar, while producing disaster distribution maps, hazard distribution maps, and susceptibility zoning maps for key counties including Womai and Motuo. The findings demonstrate that multi-source remote sensing combined with GIS evaluation models effectively addresses limitations in ground surveys and cloud-obscured data collection, providing critical support for site selection and route planning for hydropower transmission projects in southwestern China, hazard identification, monitoring network deployment, and flood control measures.

papers.title: Research on geological disaster risk assessment of highway corridors integrating multisource spatial information
papers.summary: In mountainous and tectonically active regions, geological hazards pose a significant threat to highway corridors, with serious consequences for infrastructure integrity and human safety. To address this issue, this study integrates multi-source spatial information and develops a rapid geohazard risk assessment framework based on the analytic hierarchy process (AHP), the entropy weight method, and the Technique for Order Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution (TOPSIS). The results indicate that: (1) the fusion of multisource spatial information derived from landslide density, landslide susceptibility, and InSAR deformation rate can effectively characterize the spatial heterogeneity of geological hazard risk within the highway corridor; (2) the highway corridor in the study area is dominated overall by very low- and low-hazard zones, whereas high- and very high-hazard zones are mainly distributed in linear and patchy patterns, concentrated in the central section of the route and in local areas of the southern section; and (3) the integrated evaluation approach based on AHP–entropy weighting and the TOPSIS model enables a unified quantitative representation of three indicators, thereby producing a geological hazard zonation map for the highway corridor. This framework provides technical support for highway route planning, construction, and operation in geologically complex regions.

papers.title: Extending the Martian landslide inventory southward: distribution, landslide types, and latitudinal extent
papers.summary: Martian landslide inventories remain concentrated near the equator, particularly in Valles Marineris. We present 411 previously uncatalogued landslides spanning 63°S–34°N, extending coverage of the southern mid-latitudes and increasing the existing global catalogue by approximately 13%. Most events (73.7%) occur between 20°S and 50°S, and 84.9% originate within Early and Middle Noachian highland units. Rock avalanches dominate (49.1%), followed by slumps (26.8%), rock avalanche/ejecta forms (12.2%), and slump/rock avalanche transitions (11.9%). The apparent mobility index (H/L) ranges from 0.03 to 0.31 (5th–95th percentiles) and generally decreases with landslide area, although this relationship varies by type. No significant inventory-wide relationship exists between mobility and latitude. Crater size–frequency distributions of selected deposits indicate predominantly Late Amazonian model surface ages, with older surfaces reaching 1.68 ± 0.48 Ga. This inventory provides new spatial, morphological, and chronological constraints on mass wasting beyond the well-studied canyon systems.

papers.title: Landslide susceptibility assessment in Le'an County using machine learning approaches
papers.summary: Landslide susceptibility assessment is a core pre-step in geological disaster risk Landslide susceptibility assessment is a core pre-step in geological disaster risk prevention and control. Traditional assessment methods have significant limitations in verifying the precision gain effect of factor screening and quantifying the influence of multicollinearity among multiple factors. This paper takes Le'an County in Jiangxi Province, a typical landslide-prone county in the southern red soil hilly area, as the research area. Based on a 12.5 m DEM, the research area is divided into 50,522 slope units, and a disaster-prone factor table including 15 core factors such as elevation, slope, and NDVI is constructed, forming a refined landslide susceptibility evaluation system based on slope units. Using the dual diagnostic method of Pearson correlation coefficient and variance inflation factor (VIF), 10 core evaluation factors without significant collinearity were identified. Model training and performance assessment were implemented based on the selected dataset through spatial 5-fold cross-validation. The results show that after eliminating redundant factors, the accuracy of each model has significantly improved. Specifically, the RF model outperformed the other counterparts, attaining a training accuracy of 0.824, a validation accuracy of 0.817, and an AUC of 0.84. These results markedly outperformed those of the LR model (AUC=0.74) and the SVM model (AUC=0.76). The areas with extremely high susceptibility to landslides are concentrated in the southeastern part of Le'an County, which is highly consistent with the coupled driving mechanism of topography, hydrology and soil.

papers.title: Climatology and trends of observed daily and hourly extreme precipitation in the French Alps
papers.summary: Abstract. The French Alps are characterized by complex topography, which influences precipitation regimes and associated risks in various ways. Extreme precipitation, especially when it happens on very short timescales, can lead to flash floods and landslides with important social and economic impacts. Local stakeholders, working on prevention and protection from such events, report a perceived recent increase in sub-daily extreme precipitation intensities in the French Alps. However, to our knowledge, this has not yet been confirmed statistically. In this paper, we apply a statistical approach based on extreme value theory on long time series of in situ observations. By comparing daily and hourly observations and analysing both months and seasons, we are able to present a climatology as well as trends of precipitation extremes in unprecedented detail. Here we define 'extreme' as 20-year return levels of precipitation intensity, focusing thus on very rare events. In a first part, we use a stationary framework to provide an updated climatology of daily and hourly extremes. We make use of an existing weather pattern classification to show the dynamic influences on precipitation maxima, highlighting the strong differences between the northern and the southern French Alps as well as between seasons. In a second part, we compute trends of these extremes, for which we also find partially large differences between regions and seasons. For annual extremes of daily precipitation, we find strong positive trends in the south and negative trends in the north, mostly driven by changes in autumn. Annual trends of hourly extremes are mostly non-significant and show more of an east-west division, with positive trends in the high Alps and negative ones in the pre-Alps.

papers.title: Tsunamigenic potential of flank instabilities of Kameni Volcano inside Santorini Caldera, southern Aegean
papers.summary: Located in the southern Aegean Sea, the Santorini volcanic complex represents one of the most geodynamically active and hazardous volcano–tectonic systems in the Mediterranean. Following the Late Bronze Age caldera-forming eruption (~ 1600 BCE ), the Kameni volcanic edifice emerged within the central caldera. On the northwestern flank of Nea Kameni, lava flows are superposed on unconsolidated pyroclastic deposits, primarily pumice and ash attributed to the 726 CE submarine explosive eruption. These units reside on a topographic step coincident with a major volcano–tectonic lineament, a geomorphological configuration that exhibits structural parallels to the pre−2018 sector collapse state of Anak Krakatau. Here, we employ the Landslide-HySEA numerical code to simulate tsunami generation and propagation resulting from various potential flank instability scenarios of Nea Kameni. Three distinct collapse volumes were modeled: 0.057 km 3 , 0.077 km 3 , and 0.13 km 3 . The simulations demonstrate substantial hazardous potential; a flank failure of 0.13 km 3 has the potential to generate maximum coastal wave amplitudes of up to 39 m. Furthermore, all modeled scenarios result in tsunami heights exceeding 2 m at multiple critical coastal locations. These results indicate that such events would inflict severe damage on critical infrastructure and high-density maritime hubs situated along the inner caldera cliffs. Seafloor microbathymetry acquired through a photogrammetric tow-sled system suggests little remobilization despite ongoing volcano–seismic activity. Yet, our findings underscore the necessity for continuous monitoring of the structural stability of the Kameni volcanic edifice and emphasize the requirement to integrate flank-collapse mechanisms into the tsunami hazard assessment frameworks for Santorini.

papers.title: An Optimized Method for Slope Deformation Monitoring via Parallel-Track InSAR Data Fusion
papers.summary: Abstract. This study addresses geometric distortion in SAR imagery caused by complex topography in reservoir areas, which adversely affects the accuracy of InSAR monitoring. A multi-orbit data fusion technique is proposed, integrating the R-Index(im) with an improved Geometric Distortion (GD) Index. Using the study landslide mass at Danjiangkou Reservoir as a case study, the research leverages Sentinel-1A satellite data. The GD index model is optimized by incorporating a shadow effect coefficient (Sh). Combined with the R-Index(im) 's capability for distortion-region identification, an adaptive weighted fusion model is established. Empirical analysis demonstrates that this approach effectively corrects deformation monitoring biases caused by geometric distortion. Compared to single-orbit data, the fusion results reduce deformation rate errors by 0.02 mm/year and 0.36 mm/year, while expanding the monitoring coverage by 32 %. Verification against GNSS ground-truth data confirms that this method significantly enhances the accuracy and reliability of InSAR monitoring in complex terrain, offering an effective technical solution for reservoir landslide early warning.

papers.title: Hydro-mechanical assessment of tunnel–fill slope systems under extreme rainfall: effects of foundations and slope protection
papers.summary: Tunnel excavation through fill slopes under extreme rainfall involves complex hydro-mechanical interactions among excavation-induced stress redistribution, rainfall infiltration, slope deformation, and adjacent infrastructure. This study investigates the response and stability of a tunnel–fill slope system using integrated physical model testing and numerical simulation. The physical experiments examined rainfall infiltration, ground settlement, stress redistribution, and pore-water-pressure evolution during excavation. The validation test simulated an upper-range heavy-rainfall event of 200 mm/day for 12 h at prototype scale, corresponding to approximately 16.67 mm/day applied for 1 h in the 1:120-scale model. Agreement between the experimental and numerical results confirmed the model’s ability to reproduce the principal hydraulic and deformation responses. Two parametric investigations were subsequently conducted. The first evaluated the effects of adjacent buildings and foundation systems under rainfall and dry conditions, focusing on building settlement and slope-supporting pile displacement. The second assessed riprap, geocell reinforcement, and vegetation under rainfall without building loads by examining slope deformation and pore-water-pressure development. The results demonstrate that rainfall intensifies hydro-mechanical responses and structural deformation, while the effectiveness of protection measures varies according to their hydraulic and mechanical functions. These findings support the selection of suitable foundation systems and slope-protection strategies in complex urban fill-slope environments.

papers.title: Simulation-Informed Machine Learning for Multiclass Landslide and Debris-Flow Hazard Classification in a Recently Urbanized City, Republic of Korea
papers.summary: Rapid urban expansion into mountainous terrain, together with increasing exposure to extreme weather, has increased the need for transparent and interpretable slope-hazard assessment in forested and residential mountain environments. However, relatively few studies have integrated field-survey information with physically based simulation outputs for interpretable multi-class classification within an established slope-hazard grading framework. This pilot study developed a simulation-informed machine-learning framework for classifying composite slope-hazard grades (Grades I–III) using 71 landslide-prone and 52 debris-flow-prone sites in Sejong City, Republic of Korea. For the landslide dataset, selected field-survey indicators were integrated with SoilWorks-derived slope-stability information, whereas for the debris-flow dataset, selected field-survey indicators were integrated with FLO-2D-derived simulation information. Four machine-learning algorithms—Random Forest (RF), Logistic Regression (LR), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), and Support Vector Machine (SVM)—were evaluated under severe class imbalance. RF showed the strongest overall performance in the original holdout evaluation, achieving an accuracy of 0.857 for both datasets and weighted F1-scores of 0.849 for the landslide dataset and 0.836 for the debris-flow dataset. Gini importance, Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP), and targeted ablation analysis indicated that simulation-derived variables provided strong discriminatory information within the established grading framework. papers.title: Reply on RC2
papers.summary: Abstract. Ground motion poses a significant threat to the safety and functionality of transport infrastructure, particularly in regions affected by landslides, subsidence, freeze–thaw processes, and large-scale tunnelling. Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) enables millimeter-level displacement monitoring over large areas and is used to support infrastructure risk assessment. Here, we evaluate the usability of two InSAR approaches, (i) Persistent Scatterer Interferometry (PSI) using displacement products from the European Ground Motion Service (EGMS), and (ii) a combined Persistent- and Distributed-Scatterer (PS+DS) phase-linking workflow across key Swedish transport corridors. Rather than a strictly controlled methodological comparison, we evaluate how differences between operational InSAR solutions translate into practical performance for infrastructure monitoring. Results show that PS+DS consistently yields five times as many measurement points while maintaining RMSE values within a similar range to EGMS (mostly below 6 mm in the Line Of Sight direction). The EGMS exhibits narrower RMSE distributions, but PS+DS achieves comparable median RMSE of the measurement points across most land-cover types and corridor environments. Both datasets capture similar displacement patterns along all corridors, with measurement points from both approaches concentrating within the linear corridor geometry. Overall, the five-fold increase in PS+DS point density offers infrastructure operators a practical pathway to finer-scale ground motion monitoring for railway maintenance and risk assessment, while demonstrating how the choice of operational InSAR processing strategy shapes the information available for Earth-observation-based infrastructure applications.

papers.title: Potential erosion risk assessment of Kanak stream basin (Sivas, Sarkisla) with the ICONA model
papers.source: Frontiers in Life Sciences and Related Technologies
papers.summary: The rapid development of technology following the Industrial Revolution has increased human domination over nature. Erosion, which plays a critical role in the process of natural shaping of the earth, can accelerate over time because of improper utilization of the natural environment by humans. The main objective of this study is to determine the erosion susceptibility of the Kanak Creek Basin, one of the sub-basins in the upper reaches of the Kizilirmak River, using the ICONA model, whose main parameters are slope, lithology, land use and vegetation cover, and Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and Remote Sensing techniques, and to list the measures that can be taken against erosion. According to the results of the ICONA model potential erosion level map, 48% of the study area has low erosion susceptibility. These areas largely correspond to the vicinity of Sama Mountain, which has volcanic rocks resistant to erosion, and the base of Sarkisla Plain where the slope is very low. The plain floor is largely covered with agricultural lands. The expansion of irrigated agriculture in this region is one of the main measures that can be taken against erosion. Erosion susceptibility increases around Turna Mountain on the northern border of the basin and Cal Mountain in the south due to both the increase in slope and the lack of resistance of the rocks in the region to erosion, and corresponds to 30% of the study area. In 22% of the basin, susceptibility to erosion is at a medium level. Most of these areas consist of natural meadows and pastures. It is essential to take measures against overgrazing in these areas to prevent the complete loss of the already sparse vegetation cover. Planning land use in the basin in a sustainable manner, arranging fields and layers perpendicular to the slope, expanding irrigated agriculture, and preventing overgrazing are of vital importance in terms of combating soil erosion.

papers.title: Effects of waveguide tube geometry and surrounding medium conditions on acoustic emission signal attenuation
papers.summary: Deep-seated deformation in landslides is typically concealed and exhibits a time lag; reliably obtaining information on internal deformation through acoustic emission (AE) technology remains a key challenge in landslide early warning. Metal waveguides can reduce the impact of strong soil attenuation on AE signal acquisition; however, the mechanisms of propagation attenuation within the metal waveguides themselves remain unclear. To address this, this study conducted controlled laboratory experiments on wave propagation in waveguide tubes to systematically investigate the differences in propagation attenuation caused by waveguide diameter, wall thickness, and the state of the surrounding medium. By analyzing time-domain waveforms, frequency-domain characteristics, time–frequency representations, and fitting exponential attenuation models, the study examined the attenuation changes with increasing propagation distance under different operating conditions. The results indicate that the amplitude of AE signals generally exhibits exponential attenuation as the propagation distance increases. When comparing individual factors, the surrounding-medium condition produced the largest change in attenuation, followed by outer diameter, whereas wall thickness had the weakest effect. Attenuation was also frequency selective. These findings provide a basis for selecting components for active waveguide systems (AWS), determining sensor spacing, and establishing effective monitoring ranges.

papers.title: Weather and Landslide Data Analysis Using Spatio-Temporal and Categorical Data Mining
papers.summary: This paper proposes a semantic correlation and knowledge mining method that identifies semantic correlation structures between two sets with different granularities and numbers of elements, and performs semantic interpretation and knowledge representation of coarse-grained events. When humans understand an event, we do not refer only to a single element that directly corresponds to the event. Instead, use the time before and after the event, the space in which the event occurred, and related concepts as clues. We then select semantically related subsets from a large amount of surrounding information and integrate them as the background of the event. The proposed method aims to computationally formalize this process of background exploration. The proposed method targets a set $A$, which contains many fine-grained elements, and a set $B$, which contains a small number of coarse-grained elements. For each $b_j \in B$, the method constructs a semantically related subset $A_j \subseteq A$ from set $A$. Each element is represented in a semantic space $S$ composed of time, space, and vocabulary, and the semantic correlation between the aggregated representation of the subset and the representation of $b_j$ is computed. Through this process, the proposed method explicitly describes latent correspondences between data sets with different granularities and representation formats as subset-level correlation structures, and provides a framework for transforming these structures into reusable knowledge representations. Furthermore, this paper applies the proposed method to the disaster prevention domain and demonstrates that semantic correlation structures can be constructed between meteorological observation data and landslide event data. The results confirm that the proposed method is effective for the integrated understanding of heterogeneous data sets and for knowledge extraction.

papers.title: Year-Wise Refitted Spatiotemporal Landslide Susceptibility Forecasting Driven by IMD Rainfall and SMAP Soil Moisture, Wayanad, India
papers.summary: Landslides in hilly regions threaten life, infrastructure, and ecosystems. Landslide susceptibility is inherently transient, yet conventional analysis produces time-invariant zoning and evaluates it by random partitioning of a temporally structured inventory, which permits later events to inform predictions for earlier ones. This study develops a year-wise refitted framework for the Wayanad district of the Western Ghats, India, in which a Random Forest classifier is refitted independently for each target year from 2020 to 2024 using only events recorded earlier, with all target-year events withheld from training. Dynamic susceptibility is driven by India Meteorological Department (IMD) gridded daily rainfall and NASA Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) soil moisture alongside static conditioning factors. Decomposing the evaluation set shows that the conventional random holdout returns a mean AUC-ROC of 0.913, rising monotonically, whereas withheld target-year events return 0.871 with no trend; the target-year value is lower in every year examined (sign test p = 0.031), and the divergence widens as the inventory grows. A Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (Bi-LSTM) network forecasts both triggering factors, extending susceptibility mapping to 2025 and 2026, years for which no meteorological record existed when the maps were produced. Two landslides subsequently reported in Wayanad during that period both fall within zones these maps classify as High. A cloudburst scenario is simulated to assess the response to localised extreme rainfall. The framework shifts susceptibility assessment from retrospective hindcasting to forward prediction, and makes explicit the optimism that conventional validation conceals.

papers.title: AusAEM in Tasmania: survey design and early results
papers.summary: Summary Recent helicopter-borne airborne electromagnetic (AEM) data acquisition across Tasmania has significantly expanded subsurface imaging capability for mineral, groundwater and hazard applications. Approximately 11,000 line-km of time-domain AEM data were collected under Geoscience Australia’s Resourcing Australia’s Prosperity initiative, in collaboration with Mineral Resources Tasmania. Survey design incorporated variable line spacing (10 km to 125 m) to address multiple objectives, including regional geological mapping, mineral prospectivity targeting, hydrogeology, and regolith characterisation. Inversion of the data using Geoscience Australia’s Layered Earth Inversion framework has produced conductivity models that effectively delineate key geological units and subsurface structures. Initial results demonstrate clear imaging of Jurassic dolerite and Cenozoic cover sequences, which obscure prospective basement geology. The data also highlight aquifer structures, groundwater salinity variations and landslide-related clay horizons. Case studies, including detailed acquisition over the Scotia mine area and Bass Strait islands, illustrate the value of high-resolution AEM data for environmental monitoring and geohazard assessment. The survey has apparently achieved and exceeded its design objectives, with ongoing interpretation expected to substantially advance geological understanding across Tasmania.

papers.title: Integrated Passive and Active Seismic Imaging for Landslide Characterization at Chichester Dam, NSW
papers.summary: Summary GHD undertook a multi-method seismic imaging investigation of a relict landslide system on the left abutment (looking downstream) of Chichester Dam in NSW as part of a broader periodic dam safety review. The current risk assessment identifies potential reactivation of these landslides as a dam failure mode, while uncertainty in their characterisation limits development of an accurate risk position. The investigation aims to improve understanding of the landslides and reduce this uncertainty. The seismic investigation combined complementary passive and active methods: ambient noise tomography (ANT), horizontal-to-vertical spectral ratios (HVSRs), seismic refraction tomography (SRT), and GHD’s frequency-time analysis based surface wave inversion (FTAN-SWI). These methods were selected to balance the resolution limits and spatial coverage required at the site, while also addressing environmental constraints associated with the adjacent protected environmental zone. Subsurface Vp and Vs models indicate that weaker soil/weathered rock cover is thinner around the abutment rim ( 30 m), consistent with observed mass loss around the rim. Fundamental resonance frequencies from HVSR curves show a systematic spatial pattern supporting this interpretation and may indicate areas of recent mobility along the rim, both downstream and upstream of the dam. Correlation of borehole information with Vp and Vs models suggests that the base of landslides intersect shale interbeds within sandstone, indicating a possible causal relationship between landsliding and weaker shale horizons. The ANT-derived volumetric Vs model also identifies a deeper mid-slope lower velocity zone spatially correlated with head scarps of landslides at the surface; the significance of this correlation remains uncertain. Overall, the geophysical investigation improves the landslide conceptual model and supports planning of further investigations.

papers.title: Revealing the Hydrothermal System of La Soufrière Volcano (Guadeloupe) Through Nodal Ambient Noise Tomography
papers.summary: Abstract La Soufri'ere de Guadeloupe is an active volcano of the Lesser Antilles Volcanic Arc. Its last eruption halted in 1977, yet hydrothermal activity has increased over recent years, raising summit instability hazards. The link between hydrothermal fluids and detachment landslide surfaces is well established and exacerbated by inflation, pressurization, and fluid flow lubrication. Nodal Ambient Noise Tomography offers the resolution and penetration needed to investigate such features in 3D. In 2023, we deployed 39 nodal geophones that recorded for about 1 month. The resulting 3D S‐wave velocity model resolves a central low‐velocity conduit, possible flank detachment planes, and subsurface structures of the shallow volcanic cone. Our results highlight the complex interaction between fluid transport (meteoric and magmatic) and tectono‐magmatic drivers. This provides the first high‐resolution 3D seismic imaging for slope stability assessment in volcanic environments. Understanding detachment zone geometry and distribution contributes to hazard risk assessment and mitigation.

papers.title: Acoustic emission characterization of soil shear deformation using active waveguide systems
papers.summary: Acoustic emission (AE) sensing offers a non-destructive approach for monitoring deformations in granular geomaterials with potential for landslide early warning system (LEWS). In this study, the AE characteristics generated during controlled large-scale soil shear deformation were investigated using active waveguide system (AWS) embedded in a custom-developed shear apparatus. Constant shear displacement rates ranging from 0.005 to 30.0 mm/min, along with accelerating and decelerating deformation histories, were imposed to examine the evolution of AE activity, cumulative counts, signal duration, energy, and frequency-domain characteristics across defined deformation velocity scales. Cumulative AE counts exhibited a quadratic relationship with elapsed time for all constant-rate tests. The square root of the quadratic coefficient (√β) was proportional to the imposed shear displacement rate, demonstrating the potential of cumulative AE counts for laboratory calibration of deformation velocity. Under the controlled laboratory conditions, frequency-domain analysis revealed concentrated centroid-frequency of 70-90 kHz and concentrated peak-frequency of 30-80 kHz, representing the combined response of granular source mechanisms and the soil-AWS-sensor system. Variable-rate experiments also showed the sensitivity of AE parameters to transitions between successive deformation regimes. The proposed relationships provide a laboratory-calibrated framework for non-destructive characterisation of soil shear deformation and establish a basis for future site-specific calibration of AE-based LEWS.

papers.title: Interpretable AutoML and Double Machine Learning for Landslide Susceptibility Assessment in Tongren, Qinghai–Tibet Plateau
papers.summary: Landslide susceptibility assessment in cold, high-altitude regions is complicated by interactions among topographic, lithological, hydrological, and anthropogenic factors. Machine learning methods are widely used, but model selection, spatially independent evaluation, and interpretation of covariate-adjusted associations remain challenging. This study developed an integrated framework for landslide susceptibility assessment in Tongren City, on the northeastern margin of the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau. The framework combined H2O AutoML, nested spatial cross-validation, Shapley additive explanations (SHAP), partial dependence plots (PDPs), and double machine learning (DML). Each of the 20 sampling realizations included 217 landslide points and 217 non-landslide points, with 13 conditioning factors retained after collinearity screening. DML used partially linear regression with spatial cross-fitting across 200 repetitions to estimate covariate-adjusted associations. Stacked Ensemble achieved the highest mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.953 ± 0.009 across the 20 realizations. Spatial out-of-fold evaluation showed that the 20% of the study area with the highest susceptibility contained 93.27% ± 1.51% of held-out landslides (mean ± standard deviation). Elevation, distance to roads, lithology, distance to faults, and land use/land cover together accounted for 76.69% of the total mean absolute SHAP values. PDPs revealed nonlinear relationships between conditioning factors and model-predicted susceptibility. Elevation, interpreted as a proxy for valley position, and distance to roads were the only factors with statistically significant negative covariate-adjusted associations after multiple-testing correction. The random common cause (RCC) test indicated that DML estimates remained stable under the random-covariate perturbations examined. papers.title: Smart Disaster Response Drone for Rapid Relief Operation
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Disasters such as floods, earthquakes, landslides and large-scale accidents can damage roads, power systems and communication infrastructure, delaying search, assessment and relief delivery. Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) can provide rapid aerial observation, survivor-search support, delivery of lightweight emergency supplies and temporary communication coverage. This review synthesizes three supplied papers: a global review of UAVs for search and rescue, a YOLO-based radio-frequency (RF) spectrogram detector, and a lightweight authentication protocol for emergency UAVs. The search-and-rescue literature emphasizes sensor integration, multi-UAV coordination, communication recovery and the persistent constraints of battery endurance and payload. The RF detection study compares YOLOv8n and YOLOv9t, reporting mAP50–95 values around 0.80–0.85 and inference times of 1.6 ms and 3.0 ms, respectively, in its experimental setting. The authentication study addresses mutual authentication and session-key establishment among an operational drone, ground station and rescue drones, using formal protocol analysis. These contributions are relevant but do not individually demonstrate a complete end-to-end disaster-relief platform. This review proposes a conceptual architecture combining multisensor reconnaissance, edge-based AI, task allocation across multiple UAVs, secure communications and human-supervised relief decisions. Major gaps include limited field validation, uncertain performance under severe weather and radio interference, battery and payload trade-offs, and the need to test security and detection jointly in realistic missions.

papers.title: The Geomorphology of Footwalls and Fault Scarps in Marine Rift Basins: Greater Tampen Spur Area, Northern North Sea
papers.summary: ABSTRACT This study investigates the footwall crest and fault scarp geomorphology of crustal‐scale fault blocks developed during Late Jurassic rifting on the Greater Tampen Spur, northern North Sea, using 3D seismic data and 84 exploration wells. The Snorre and Visund footwalls represent contrasting geomorphic end members. Snorre is characterised by a broad, plateau‐like erosion surface that truncates tilted Triassic strata and its fault scarp comprises degraded slopes, centrally developed U‐shaped gullies and canyons and hanging‐wall rider blocks developed in an area of overlapping fault segments. The Visund footwall, in contrast, is convex‐up and asymmetric, locally preserves Late Jurassic strata at its crest and is associated with a steep fault scarp containing structurally guided V‐shaped gullies and canyons, larger U‐shaped canyons and a large submarine landslide. These contrasting morphologies reflect different balances between fault‐related uplift, regional subsidence and the timing and duration of drowning. At Snorre, large displacement on the Snorre–Zeta Fault, combined with additional uplift from west‐dipping faults bounding the Marulk Basin, kept the footwall at shallow levels long enough for prolonged wave ravinement. At Visund, local footwall uplift was offset by hanging‐wall subsidence related to the Snorre–Zeta Fault system and by greater regional tectonic subsidence toward the North Viking Graben. This lower structural position led to earlier drowning, favouring submarine diffusive hillslope retreat, repeated mass wasting and preservation of fault‐scarp incisions. Together, these results show that displacement history, structural position within a fault network, drowning history, bedrock lithology, secondary faulting and geomorphic preservation collectively govern footwall and fault‐scarp morphology in marine rift basins. papers.title: A comprehensive review of 3D digital mapping-based automated rock discontinuity detection: emerging technologies, challenges and future prospects
papers.summary: Accurate detection and characterization of rock discontinuities are essential for rock slope stability assessment, tunnel excavation, rockfall hazard evaluation and rock mass classification. Conventional field methods, including geological compass measurements, scanline surveys and manual mapping, remain important but are limited by restricted spatial coverage, operator subjectivity, time consumption and safety risks in steep or inaccessible rock masses. This review critically examines recent progress in automated and semi-automated rock discontinuity detection using 3D digital mapping, advanced remote sensing and artificial intelligence-based methods. The reviewed detection approaches include LiDAR-based terrestrial and aerial laser scanning, UAV photogrammetry, hyperspectral imaging, 3D point-cloud processing and classical image-processing techniques such as edge detection. Particular emphasis is placed on AI-driven discontinuity detection, including convolutional neural networks for 2D image-based recognition, semantic segmentation models such as U-Net and DeepLabV3+, object and instance segmentation frameworks such as YOLO, Faster R-CNN, Mask R-CNN, Mask R-CNN–TD and YOLACT++, and advanced architectures including 3D point-cloud networks, transformer-based models, graph neural networks, transfer learning and hybrid 2D–3D fusion models such as CNN–PointNet. This review shows that LiDAR- and UAV-derived point clouds can provide reliable discontinuity orientation, spacing, joint-set and block-geometry information, supporting stereonet-based kinematic analysis, rock mass quality assessment, RQD estimation and identification of potentially unstable blocks. papers.title: Reply on RC1
papers.summary: Abstract. Tectonic suture zones on the Tibetan Plateau, as structurally weak belts, commonly host numerous large to very large rockslides. However, how the material composition and structural architecture of suture zones govern the initiation and evolution of landslides remains poorly understood. This study focuses on the Jinsha River suture zone (JSSZ). Through systematic field geological investigations, laboratory microstructural analyses, and landslide inventory statistics, we elucidate the control of tectonic mélange belt lithology and structure on landslide development, and construct a four-stage dynamic conceptual model from initiation to triggering. The results indicate that the heterogeneous, weak lithologies and complex structures of the suture zone provide the fundamental material and structural basis for landslide initiation. Sliding surfaces are not randomly distributed but predominantly localized along sub-horizontal foliation planes or lithological interfaces. These pre-existing discontinuities, under tectonic uplift and river incision, become preferential pathways for stress release and progressive weakening, resulting in clustered landslide distribution along the suture zone. Accordingly, a four-stage initiation and evolution model is proposed, systematically explaining the complete dynamic process from suture zone formation establishing the material-structural framework, through tectonic uplift and river incision driving rock mass fracturing, freeze–thaw cycles and chemical weathering causing progressive coalescence of the sliding surface, to final triggering of catastrophic failure. This study reveals the fundamental control of suture zone lithology and structure on landslide initiation, shifting the analytical perspective from short-term triggers to long-term dynamic coupling, and from external driving conditions to intrinsic lithological-structural constraints. The findings provide a new theoretical framework for understanding clustered rockslide

Community Social Capital and Disaster Resilience in Rural Indonesia: An Integrative Social Science Review
papers.summary: Disaster outcomes in rural Indonesia are shaped not only by the intensity of hazards but also by the social relationships through which communities communicate, cooperate, and access resources. This integrative review examined how community social capital contributes to disaster resilience in rural Indonesia and under what conditions it fails to do so. A purposive corpus of 39 sources (22 peer-reviewed articles, 5 scholarly books or chapters, 3 national regulations, and 9 institutional documents) was identified through 150 database, giving priority to publications from 2016 to 2026 while retaining foundational works. The sources were synthesized thematically using four analytical categories: bonding, bridging, and linking social capital, and participatory knowledge. The synthesis indicated that bonding ties accelerate information sharing, mutual assistance, and psychosocial support in the first hours after a hazard strikes, although most of this evidence comes from outside Indonesia. However, dense internal networks may exclude women, migrants, persons with disabilities, poor households, and other groups with weaker access to community institutions. Bridging and linking relationships are therefore needed to widen participation and to connect villages with government agencies, health services, humanitarian organizations, and technical expertise. Local knowledge was most useful when it was documented and integrated with scientific risk information through participatory planning. Situation reports from the 2025–2026 floods and landslides in Sumatra are consistent with the need for multisectoral coordination and institutional learning. The review proposes a social resilience chain, a conceptual framework not yet tested empirically, that links trust, communication, coordination, collective action, and reflective learning, and concludes that rural resilience is a social process requiring investment in relationships alongside infrastructure and early-warning systems.

Activity and Rainfall Response of the Gimigliano Landslide (Southern Italy): Insights from SBAS-InSAR Data Analysis
papers.summary: Slow-moving landslides are complex systems characterized by marked spatial and temporal variability in deformation, which may be difficult to capture using landslide-wide displacement measures. This study investigates the Gimigliano landslide (Calabria, southern Italy), a large, long-lived and urbanized slope instability, by integrating multi-temporal Sentinel-1 SBAS-InSAR observations, data-driven kinematic segmentation, geomorphological analysis and rainfall–deformation relationships. InSAR time series were clustered to identify spatially coherent kinematic domains, which were subsequently compared with independently mapped geomorphological sectors. Continuous and event-based analyses were then used to investigate the temporal relationship between rainfall and landslide deformation. Four kinematic domains were identified, with the highest domain-averaged deformation rates reaching approximately −12.8 mm/yr in the vertical component and −4.8 mm/yr in the east–west component. The identified domains show a clear spatial correspondence with the geomorphological elements of the landslide. Rainfall–deformation relationships showed the highest-magnitude correlations for 60–120 days rainfall accumulation windows, with maximum correlations occurring at lags of approximately 30–35 days for the vertical component and 60–75 days for the east–west component. Event-based analysis further highlighted variable response magnitudes among domains and delayed responses within a few weeks. The results indicate that deformation is associated with antecedent hydrological conditions while retaining substantial spatial heterogeneity, highlighting the value of integrating InSAR, geomorphological and rainfall information for the interpretation of slow-moving landslide dynamics.

papers.title: Shallow landslide diagnostics for Southern California
papers.summary: Shallow landslides are significant natural hazards in the mountainous regions of Southern California during anomalously wet winter seasons, posing substantial risks to life and property. Better understanding and operational prediction of the atmospheric and land-surface conditions leading to the initiation of these impactful events are critical for mitigating life loss and reducing damage costs. This study aims to characterize and provide templates for operational prediction of the triggering conditions of shallow landslides in Southern California with the application of the MHEBC, a decade-long, high-resolution, prototype dataset of quantitative precipitation estimates. This dataset has region-specific calibration and is the result of methodologies tailored to capture the orographic signal of precipitation, which is a key element for the generation of the precipitation associated with landslide occurrence in this region. Using recorded landslide events from the California Geological Survey Reported Landslides Database, rainfall thresholds for landslide occurrence are derived on the basis of the MHEBC dataset. Significant quality control was necessary for both rainfall and landslide databases before high-quality data input could be provided for the analysis. Observed local landslide data availability is typically limited worldwide, and Southern California is no exception. Near-complete 3D deformation mapping from Sentinel-1 through extended burst overlap interferometry
papers.summary: Despite the widespread application of satellite radar interferometry (InSAR) for measuring surface deformation, the inability to retrieve precise three-dimensional (3D) displacement remains the fundamental limitation, restricting our ability to fully characterise Earth dynamics. Here, we present a new way to recover near-complete (∼86%) 3D displacement fields from Sentinel-1. The method exploits burst overlap regions, which we extend across-and along-track, increasing the usable overlap area by 800%. We apply the approach to glacier and earthquake case studies and demonstrate that the north–south component of displacement can be robustly retrieved with a precision of 40 mm, a factorof-10 improvement over the standard approach incorporating radar intensity offset estimation (410 mm). By providing routine retrieval of the full displacement vector from Sentinel-1 InSAR, our approach enables improved quantification of rapid events, such as earthquakes and magmatic intrusions, and longer-term processes, including interseismic strain accumulation, slow-moving landslides and glacier flow.

papers.title: Shaking table investigation into seismic failure mechanisms of bedrock-underlain stratified slopes: influence of soil layer configuration
papers.summary: Soil layer configuration governs the seismic failure characteristics and dynamic responses of layered slopes. However, the seismic damage evolution and mechanical mechanisms of clay-over-sand and sand-over-clay slopes remain poorly understood. This study integrates shaking table tests and cyclic triaxial tests to investigate how soil layer distribution controls slope failure mode, acceleration amplification, and dynamic stress evolution. The results indicate that: (1) Differences in soil mechanical properties across layers give rise to distinct seismic damage patterns. The upper-clay/lower-sand slope exhibits progressive plastic sliding with significant accumulated deformation, whereas the upper-sand/lower-clay slope undergoes brittle failure characterized by surface tensile cracking and shallow instantaneous sliding. (2) The acceleration amplification factor increases nonlinearly with peak ground acceleration (PGA), peaking no later than the critical state and decreasing sharply once the slope fails, thereby serving as a precursor to seismically-induced slope instability. (3) Soil layer configuration governs the spatial evolution of dynamic stress. In the upper-clay/lower-sand slope, the soft clay layer in the upper-middle section exhibits large stress fluctuations and frequent redistribution, forming the primary damage zone. In the upper-sand/lower-clay slope, the lower clay layer serves as a stable basal boundary, intensifying dynamic stress responses in the middle-lower section; slope stability is governed by basal restraint. (4) Quantitative stress–volumetric strain constitutive models were developed from triaxial tests at varying confining pressures, elucidating the transition from dilative behavior at low pressures to contractive behavior at high pressures and revealing how confining pressure governs soil deformation and failure. This study advances the understanding of seismic instability mechanisms in layered soil slopes and informs seismic reinforcement st

papers.title: Coseismic rock slope deformation at different failure stages - towards assessing the likelihood of high hazard avalanching failures
papers.summary: Landslide hazard is the probability of occurrence of an event of a given magnitude in a specific area and time period. The failure mechanism of the mass, and displacement needed to transition the hillslope from metastable to failure are fundamental inputs for coseismic landslide hazard analyses. In closely-jointed rock mass, joint-step-path failure mechanisms evolve with increasing rock-mass displacement. Three main stages have been hypothesized; incipient, transitional and avalanching. Investigating and characterizing these failure-stage transitions is critical for quantifying coseismic landslide hazard as the hillslope-specific scale. However, little is known about the magnitudes of rock mass displacement associated with these transitions. This study aims to quantify the hillslope displacement magnitudes required to transition a rock mass to failure. These thresholds are based on remote sensing measurements of displacement and derived estimates of normalised translational slope displacement (TSDs) - used as a proxy for rock mass deformation or strain - for six coseismic landslides situated in closely-jointed greywacke. Our results show that for a rock mass to transition from metastable to failure - the rock avalanche stage - requires TSDs greater than 5%, where the amount of TSD required varies with the hillslope angle. We propose an empirically-derived “translational slope deformation index” (TSDI); a function of the translational angle of displacement and normalised displacement along it. This novel tool could provide the link between the permanent slope displacements estimated using analytical methods, to the likelihood that a slope will transition into a more mobile, hazardous rock avalanche, during earthquake shaking.

papers.title: Landslide Susceptibility Mapping Using RF ‐Reconstructed SBAS ‐ InSAR Deformation and Ensemble Learning in Wanzhou District, Chongqing, China
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Accurate landslide susceptibility assessment in mountainous regions is often constrained by the reliance on static environmental factors and by spatial discontinuities in SBAS‐InSAR‐derived deformation caused by decorrelation. To address this widely encountered problem in vegetated and topographically complex landslide‐prone regions, this study proposes a potentially transferable workflow for static‐deformation‐informed landslide susceptibility assessment that integrates SBAS‐InSAR deformation reconstructed using a standard random forest (RF) regression model with ensemble machine learning. Wanzhou District, Chongqing, China, located within the Three Gorges Reservoir Area, was selected as a representative mountainous study area influenced by reservoir‐related hydrological processes. Mean line‐of‐sight deformation rates were retrieved from ascending Sentinel‐1A SAR images acquired between January 2020 and December 2024. Fifteen static conditioning factors and a historical landslide inventory were compiled, and RF regression was used to reconstruct deformation in low‐coherence areas. The reconstructed deformation field was then incorporated as a multi‐year deformation‐based conditioning factor into landslide susceptibility modelling. Four models, including RF, XGBoost, LightGBM, and Stacking, were developed under static‐only and static‐deformation‐informed scenarios. The results show that incorporating InSAR‐derived deformation generally improved model performance, with the InSAR–Stacking model achieving the highest AUC of 0.9082. Frequency ratio analysis indicated that historical landslides were more strongly concentrated in high‐ and very‐high‐susceptibility classes under the static‐deformation‐informed framework. SHAP analysis further confirmed that deformation provides complementary information beyond conventional static factors. The two GeoPackages are the national high-susceptibility layers produced by stage 01 (01_download_susceptibility_maps/04_dissolve_high_susceptibility.R) from the municipal susceptibility maps published by the Serviço Geológico do Brasil (SGB/CPRM) in the RIGEO repository. papers.title: Research Progress and Prospect of Investigation and Monitoring Technology for Coastal Zone Geological Environment
papers.summary: ABSTRACT The coastal zone, as a dynamic interface where the lithosphere, hydrosphere, biosphere and atmosphere interact, represents a vital area for national economic and social development whilst facing escalating geological challenges and disaster risks. This review systematically synthesizes recent technological advancements in geological environment investigation and monitoring within coastal zone. It focuses on innovations in high‐resolution seismic profiling, multi‐beam bathymetry, in situ testing and sensor networks that have significantly enhanced the precision of submarine structural mapping, hazard identification and resource assessment. A major achievement is the establishment of an integrated three‐dimensional (space–air–land–sea–well) observation framework, which synergistically combines satellite remote sensing, unmanned aerial vehicles, survey vessels, seafloor observatories and borehole systems to enable comprehensive spatiotemporal surveillance. This framework has been applied to developing early warning capabilities for typical geohazards, including coastal erosion, seawater intrusion and submarine landslides. The paper also critically examines existing technical bottlenecks, such as data fusion, real‐time transmission and precursor quantification, and projects future directions towards intelligent sensing, process‐oriented mechanistic studies, cross‐platform integration, standardization and international cooperation. Distinct from prior reviews, this work provides a critical assessment of both technological innovations and practical implementations in China's coastal zones, offering a holistic perspective that addresses unresolved challenges and emerging trends, with the ultimate goal of supporting coastal engineering safety, sustainable resource utilization and ecological protection.

papers.summary: Annual satellite products, such as the AlphaEarth Foundations and TESSERA embeddings, summarize a calendar year, so the product of a landslide's event year also contains post-event observations. We audited this post-event information in 18 dated events (7 earthquakes, 11 rainstorms; 61,402 landslides), changing only the input year within each event and keeping the points, spatial folds, models and bootstrap clusters fixed. Replacing the prior-year AlphaEarth product with the event-year product raised the out-of-fold AUC by 0.087 (95% CI 0.065–0.110; all 18 events) for a point model and by 0.071 (0.048–0.093) for a patch CNN. The point-model gain was 0.085 after subtracting each event's drift between two pre-event years. On complete maps, the event-year input added on average 0.21–0.22 of the landslide area to the map's top 10% (9 of 9 events; up to 0.46). A training-year × prediction-year decomposition traced the inflation to models that learn the event's surface changes, chiefly its landslide scars; event-year inputs used only at prediction did not inflate within-event scores on average. The inflation grew with the post-event fraction of the year, reaching half its full size when 23–39% of the year followed the event; this relation survived corrections for recovery. TESSERA and plain Sentinel-2 composites behaved alike. In forward tests in three regions, models trained on earlier landslides scored 0.02–0.11 higher AUC on the new event with event-year inputs, whereas legitimate pre-event embeddings helped mainly near earlier landslides. Studies should use only products whose year ends before the event.
